name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Definition of biotechnology given by EFB

questiontext.text: According to the European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB), which definition encompasses both the traditional view and modern molecular biotechnology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biotechnology encompasses both traditional microbe-mediated processes and modern recombinant DNA techniques.

Step 2: EFB Definition
The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) formulated a unified definition that bridges both traditional view and modern molecular biotechnology as: 'The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services'.

Final Answer:
The definition provided by the European Federation of Biotechnology is the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services.

answer.text: The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services
The technique of using live micro-organisms solely for the production of food items on a domestic scale
The manipulation of genes in eukaryotic cells strictly for medical therapeutic purposes
The synthesis of artificial genes and their random insertion into host plant chromosomes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Recognition sequence property of restriction endonucleases

questiontext.text: Restriction endonucleases identify a specific sequence in DNA to make cuts. What is the nature of this recognition site?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Enzymatic Characterization
Restriction endonucleases function by inspecting the length of double-stranded DNA molecules until they locate their specific target sites.

Step 2: Recognition Sequence
Each restriction endonuclease recognizes a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence in DNA, where the sequence reads the same on both strands when read in the same orientation.

Final Answer:
The recognition sequence of a restriction endonuclease is a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence.

answer.text: A tandemly repeated poly-A sequence
A specific palindromic nucleotide sequence
A random non-specific GC-rich sequence
A single-stranded protruding RNA sequence

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - First restriction endonuclease isolated and characterized

questiontext.text: Which enzyme was the first restriction endonuclease to be isolated and characterized, whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Context
Two enzymes restricting bacteriophage growth in Escherichia coli were initially discovered in 1963, one of which cut DNA.

Step 2: Identification of Hind II
Five years later, the first restriction endonuclease whose action depended on a specific six-base-pair recognition sequence was isolated and characterized as Hind II.

Final Answer:
The first restriction endonuclease isolated and characterized based on a specific recognition sequence is Hind II.

answer.text: EcoRI
BamHI
Hind II
Sal I

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Enzyme responsible for joining cut DNA

questiontext.text: In recombinant DNA technology, which enzyme is utilized to link the cut alien DNA fragment with the cut vector DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ligation Mechanism
Restriction endonucleases cut DNA strands leaving sticky ends with complementary overhanging bases.

Step 2: Enzyme Action
DNA ligase acts on these cut DNA molecules and joins their sugar-phosphate backbones end-to-end to create a continuous recombinant DNA molecule.

Final Answer:
The enzyme used to join the ends of cut DNA fragments is DNA ligase.

answer.text: DNA polymerase
Exonuclease
RNA polymerase
DNA ligase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Matrix commonly used in gel electrophoresis

questiontext.text: Which natural polymer extracted from seaweeds is the most commonly used matrix in gel electrophoresis for separating DNA fragments?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Separation Technique
Gel electrophoresis is used to resolve DNA fragments produced by restriction endonuclease digestion.

Step 2: Matrix Material
The matrix commonly used for this separation is agarose, which is a natural polysaccharide polymer extracted from seaweeds.

Final Answer:
The commonly used gel matrix extracted from seaweeds is agarose.

answer.text: Agarose
Cellulose
Polyacrylamide
Dextran

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Migration direction of DNA during electrophoresis

questiontext.text: During agarose gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments migrate toward the anode (positive electrode)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical Nature of DNA
DNA molecules possess a sugar-phosphate backbone where the ionized phosphate groups confer a net negative charge.

Step 2: Electrophoretic Mobility
Under an applied electric field, negatively charged DNA fragments are repelled by the cathode and migrate toward the positively charged anode.

Final Answer:
DNA fragments move toward the anode because they carry a net negative charge.

answer.text: Because DNA fragments are positively charged due to histone proteins
Because DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules due to phosphate groups
Because the electrical current alters the spatial conformation of DNA
Because agarose gel carries a net positive charge that repels DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Staining and visualization of separated DNA

questiontext.text: Separated DNA fragments in an agarose gel can only be visualized after staining with which specific compound followed by exposure to ultraviolet radiation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Visualization Principle
Pure DNA fragments are completely invisible in ordinary visible light without appropriate fluorochrome staining.

Step 2: Detection Compound
Staining the gel with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light allows the DNA fragments to be visualized as bright orange-coloured bands.

Final Answer:
Separated DNA fragments are visualized after staining with ethidium bromide followed by UV light exposure.

answer.text: Methylene blue
Acetocarmine
Ethidium bromide
Bromophenol blue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Role of origin of replication sequence

questiontext.text: What is the primary function of the origin of replication (ori) sequence present within a cloning vector?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Ori
The origin of replication is a specific DNA sequence in a chromosome or vector where replication begins.

Step 2: Dual Role
Any DNA segment linked to this sequence can replicate in the host cell, and this sequence also regulates the copy number of the linked alien DNA.

Final Answer:
The origin of replication initiates DNA replication and controls the copy number of the cloned target DNA.

answer.text: To code for proteins that degrade contaminating bacterial enzymes
To act as a selectable marker by conferring antibiotic resistance
To provide unique restriction sites for foreign gene insertion
To initiate replication and control the copy number of the linked DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Enzymatic breakdown of fungal cell wall

questiontext.text: Which enzyme is employed during the isolation of genetic material to break open the cell wall of a fungus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cell Wall Composition
The cell wall of fungi is primarily composed of chitin, a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine.

Step 2: Enzymatic Digestion
To release nucleic acids, fungal cells are treated with chitinase to degrade their chitinous cell wall.

Final Answer:
Chitinase is the specific enzyme used to digest the cell wall of fungi.

answer.text: Chitinase
Lysozyme
Cellulase
Ribonuclease

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Precipitation of purified DNA using ethanol

questiontext.text: During the extraction and purification of genetic material, purified DNA precipitates out after the addition of which substance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Precipitation Principle
After cellular proteins, RNA, and lipids are removed by enzymatic digestions, DNA remains dissolved in the aqueous solution.

Step 2: Effect of Cold Alcohol
The addition of chilled ethanol reduces the dielectric constant and dehydrates the DNA, causing it to precipitate as fine white threads that can be spooled out.

Final Answer:
Purified DNA precipitates out as fine threads upon the addition of chilled ethanol.

answer.text: Warm methanol
Chilled ethanol
Concentrated hydrochloric acid
Sodium chloride at room temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q11 - Two core techniques enabling modern biotechnology

questiontext.text: Which two core techniques enabled the birth and development of modern biotechnology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Technological Foundation
Modern biotechnology relies on two fundamental disciplines working in tandem.

Step 2: Identification of Core Techniques
Genetic engineering alters the chemistry of genetic material to change host phenotypes, while bioprocess engineering maintains a sterile environment to culture desired cells on an industrial scale.

Final Answer:
The two core techniques are genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering.

answer.text: Asexual reproduction and traditional animal cross-breeding
Microscopy and industrial ethanol distillation
Genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering
Somatic hybridization and chemical mutagenesis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q12 - Construction of first artificial recombinant DNA

questiontext.text: In 1972, Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer constructed the first artificial recombinant DNA molecule by linking an antibiotic resistance gene with a native plasmid of which organism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Breakthrough
Cohen and Boyer isolated an antibiotic resistance gene by cutting plasmid DNA with restriction enzymes.

Step 2: Source of Native Plasmid
They ligated this gene into the native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium, before transferring the resulting recombinant DNA into Escherichia coli for replication.

Final Answer:
The native plasmid used to construct the first recombinant DNA molecule was derived from Salmonella typhimurium.

answer.text: Escherichia coli
Bacillus thuringiensis
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Salmonella typhimurium

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q13 - Sequential basic steps in genetic modification

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of the three basic steps involved in genetically modifying an organism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Process Sequence
Genetic modification follows a logical linear pipeline to generate stable transgenic lineages.

Step 2: Three Key Stages
The first step is identifying DNA with desirable genes; the second step is introducing this DNA into a recipient host; and the third step is maintaining the DNA in the host and ensuring its stable transmission to progeny cells.

Final Answer:
The correct sequence is identification of DNA with desirable genes, introduction into the host, and maintenance of DNA in the host and transfer to progeny.

answer.text: Identification of DNA with desirable genes, followed by introduction of the identified DNA into the host, and maintenance of introduced DNA in the host with transfer to progeny
Introduction of foreign DNA into host, followed by identification of desirable genes, and downstream processing of synthesized proteins
Maintenance of DNA in progeny, followed by introduction of identified DNA into the host, and isolation of host chromosomes
Fragmentation of host DNA, followed by identification of alien DNA, and immediate industrial bioreactor culturing

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q14 - Derivation of name in restriction enzyme

questiontext.text: In the nomenclature of the restriction enzyme EcoRI, what does the Roman numeral 'I' indicate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nomenclature Rules
In restriction enzyme nomenclature, the first letter is the genus (E for Escherichia), the next two letters represent the species (co for coli), and the letter R represents the strain (RY 13).

Step 2: Significance of Roman Numeral
The Roman numerals following these letters designate the chronological order in which different enzymes were isolated from that particular strain of bacteria.

Final Answer:
The Roman numeral indicates the order in which the enzyme was isolated from that strain of bacteria.

answer.text: The number of recognition sequences present in the viral genome
The order in which the enzyme was isolated from that bacterial strain
The number of subunits making up the functional endonuclease
The generation of the Escherichia coli mutant strain used

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q15 - Functional distinction between exonucleases and endonucleases

questiontext.text: How do exonucleases differ fundamentally from endonucleases in their cleavage activity on nucleic acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nuclease Classification
Nucleases are enzymes that cleave nucleic acid chains and are divided into two main classes based on site of cleavage.

Step 2: Mode of Action
Exonucleases progressively remove terminal nucleotides from the free ends of DNA strands, whereas endonucleases cleave internal phosphodiester bonds at specific locations within the DNA molecule.

Final Answer:
Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the terminal ends of DNA, while endonucleases cut at specific internal positions.

answer.text: Exonucleases cut specifically within double-stranded RNA, whereas endonucleases cut only single-stranded DNA
Exonucleases break hydrogen bonds between base pairs, whereas endonucleases hydrolyze phosphodiester bonds
Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA, whereas endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within DNA
Exonucleases join broken sugar-phosphate backbones, whereas endonucleases degrade intact plasmids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q16 - Palindromic recognition sequence of enzyme EcoRI

questiontext.text: Which of the following DNA sequences represents the specific palindromic recognition sequence cleaved by the restriction endonuclease EcoRI?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Palindromic Symmetry
A palindromic DNA sequence possesses twofold rotational symmetry such that it reads identically on both antiparallel strands in the \(5' \rightarrow 3'\) direction.

Step 2: EcoRI Specificity
EcoRI recognizes the hexanucleotide sequence \(5'-\text{GAATTC}-3'\) on one strand and \(3'-\text{CTTAAG}-5'\) on the complementary strand.

Final Answer:
The recognition sequence of EcoRI is \(5'-\text{GAATTC}-3'\) and \(3'-\text{CTTAAG}-5'\).

answer.text: \(5'-\text{AAGCTT}-3'\) and \(3'-\text{TTCGAA}-5'\)
\(5'-\text{GGATCC}-3'\) and \(3'-\text{CCTAGG}-5'\)
\(5'-\text{GTCGAC}-3'\) and \(3'-\text{CAGCTG}-5'\)
\(5'-\text{GAATTC}-3'\) and \(3'-\text{CTTAAG}-5'\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q17 - Generation of sticky ends by restriction

questiontext.text: Why are the single-stranded overhanging ends produced by restriction endonucleases like EcoRI termed 'sticky ends'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cleavage Mechanism
Restriction enzymes cut each of the two strands a little away from the center of the palindrome site, between the same two bases on opposite strands.

Step 2: Sticky Ends Function
This staggered cleavage leaves short, single-stranded overhanging stretches that easily form complementary hydrogen bonds with matching cut fragments, greatly facilitating the action of DNA ligase.

Final Answer:
They are called sticky ends because they readily form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts.

answer.text: Because they readily form hydrogen bonds with complementary base sequences on counterpart cut fragments
Because they chemically bind tightly to the agarose matrix during gel electrophoresis
Because they are coated with a sticky layer of histone and non-histone proteins
Because they permanently prevent DNA ligase from linking any adjacent nucleotides

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q18 - Sieving effect and DNA fragment resolution

questiontext.text: In agarose gel electrophoresis, how are DNA fragments resolved according to their molecular size?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Charge-to-Mass Ratio
All DNA fragments possess a constant charge-to-mass ratio, meaning electrical force per unit mass is uniform.

Step 2: Sieving Effect
The agarose matrix acts as a molecular sieve; smaller fragments easily weave through the gel pores and migrate farther, whereas larger fragments face greater resistance and remain closer to the wells.

Final Answer:
Smaller DNA fragments travel farther through the agarose gel due to the sieving effect of the gel matrix.

answer.text: Larger fragments move faster because they carry a higher cumulative negative charge
Smaller fragments move farther because of the sieving effect provided by the porous agarose gel
All fragments migrate at an identical velocity regardless of their base-pair length
Circular fragments move slower than linear fragments of identical mass because of positive charge attraction

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q19 - Definition and purpose of DNA elution

questiontext.text: In recombinant DNA workflows, what does the term 'elution' refer to during agarose gel electrophoresis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Band Identification
After electrophoresis and ethidium bromide staining, the DNA band of interest is visualized under UV illumination.

Step 2: Elution Process
The band containing the desired DNA fragment is physically excised from the agarose gel slab, and the DNA is extracted and purified from the gel matrix in a process termed elution.

Final Answer:
Elution is the cutting out and extraction of separated DNA bands from the agarose gel piece.

answer.text: The loading of digested DNA samples into the cathode wells of an agarose gel
The exposure of an ethidium bromide-stained gel to ultraviolet light
The cutting out of separated DNA bands from the gel and extracting DNA from the gel piece
The precipitation of purified genomic DNA using chilled ethanol and a glass rod

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q20 - Function of selectable markers in plasmids

questiontext.text: What is the primary role of a selectable marker present in a cloning vector such as pBR322?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Transformation Efficiency
Bacterial transformation is an inefficient process where only a small minority of host cells actually take up plasmid molecules.

Step 2: Marker Action
A selectable marker (such as a gene conferring resistance to ampicillin or tetracycline) allows researchers to kill non-transformants and selectively grow only transformed bacteria.

Final Answer:
Selectable markers function to identify and eliminate non-transformants while selectively permitting the growth of transformants.

answer.text: To promote maximum transcription of downstream human genes
To terminate plasmid DNA replication once high copy numbers are achieved
To code for proteins that actively replicate the bacterial chromosomal DNA
To help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants while selectively permitting transformants to grow

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q21 - Insertional inactivation at BamHI in pBR322

questiontext.text: If a foreign DNA fragment is ligated into the BamHI restriction site of vector pBR322, what phenotypic change occurs in the resulting recombinant plasmid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Location of BamHI Site
In the cloning vector pBR322, the recognition site for BamHI is located within the coding sequence of the tetracycline resistance gene (\(tet^R\)).

Step 2: Insertional Inactivation
Ligation of foreign DNA at this BamHI site disrupts the \(tet^R\) reading frame, inactivating tetracycline resistance while leaving the ampicillin resistance gene (\(amp^R\)) intact and functional.

Final Answer:
The recombinant plasmid loses tetracycline resistance but retains ampicillin resistance.

answer.text: It loses tetracycline resistance while retaining ampicillin resistance
It loses ampicillin resistance while retaining tetracycline resistance
It loses both ampicillin and tetracycline resistance simultaneously
It gains resistance to kanamycin while retaining ampicillin resistance

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q22 - Colony colour in insertional inactivation screening

questiontext.text: In recombinant screening utilizing the \(\beta\)-galactosidase gene and a chromogenic substrate, what indicates a recombinant bacterial colony?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reporter Enzyme Action
Non-recombinant plasmids have an intact \(\beta\)-galactosidase gene, producing active enzyme that hydrolyzes the chromogenic substrate to form blue colonies.

Step 2: Insertional Inactivation
Insertion of foreign DNA into the coding sequence of \(\beta\)-galactosidase disrupts its expression, preventing color production so that recombinant colonies remain white or colorless.

Final Answer:
Recombinant colonies appear white or colorless because of the insertional inactivation of the \(\beta\)-galactosidase gene.

answer.text: Development of a deep blue color due to functional \(\beta\)-galactosidase synthesis
Formation of white or colorless colonies due to insertional inactivation of \(\beta\)-galactosidase
Complete failure of bacterial cells to divide on any nutrient agar medium
Fluorescence of bacterial colonies under long-wave ultraviolet radiation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q23 - Function of rop gene in pBR322

questiontext.text: What is the biological function of the 'rop' sequence present in the Escherichia coli cloning vector pBR322?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vector Structure
The pBR322 plasmid contains several specialized regions including antibiotic markers, origin of replication, and the rop region.

Step 2: Rop Gene Role
The rop gene specifically encodes proteins involved in the control and regulation of plasmid replication.

Final Answer:
The rop sequence codes for proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid.

answer.text: It codes for a restriction endonuclease that cleaves foreign plasmids
It encodes an antibiotic pump conferring resistance to chloramphenicol
It codes for proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid
It acts as a primary promoter for foreign eukaryotic gene transcription

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q24 - Agrobacterium tumefaciens as plant cloning vector

questiontext.text: How has the tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid of the plant pathogen Agrobacterium tumefaciens been modified for use as a cloning vector in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Natural Mechanism
Wild Agrobacterium tumefaciens uses its Ti plasmid to deliver a segment called T-DNA into dicot plant cells, causing crown gall tumors.

Step 2: Vector Modification
Genetic engineers disarmed the Ti plasmid by removing the tumor-causing genes while keeping the transfer machinery intact, allowing desired genes to be ferried into plant cells without causing disease.

Final Answer:
The Ti plasmid is modified by disarming it so that it ceases to be pathogenic while remaining capable of transferring foreign genes.

answer.text: By mutating its origin of replication so that it replicates only in animal host cells
By inserting human insulin genes into its virulence region to eliminate infection
By replacing its T-DNA with bacteriophage viral coat proteins to induce cell lysis
By disarming the plasmid so that it is no longer pathogenic while retaining its ability to transfer DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q25 - Disarmed retroviruses as animal gene vectors

questiontext.text: Why are retroviruses widely employed as vectors for delivering genes of interest into animal cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pathogenic Precedent
Naturally occurring retroviruses infect animal cells and can transform normal cells into cancerous cells by integrating their genome into the host chromosome.

Step 2: Vector Application
By disarming retroviruses—removing their oncogenic sequences while retaining their host cell infection and DNA integration mechanisms—they serve as vectors to deliver desirable genes into animal hosts.

Final Answer:
Disarmed retroviruses are used because they transfer and integrate desirable genes into animal genomes without causing transformation to cancerous states.

answer.text: Because disarmed retroviruses can efficiently integrate foreign genetic material into host genomes without causing oncogenic transformation
Because retroviruses produce chitinase enzymes that degrade animal cell membranes
Because retroviruses cannot replicate and thus remain harmlessly in the cytoplasm
Because retroviruses replicate only when heated to 42 degrees Celsius in culture

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q26 - Role of calcium ions in bacterial competence

questiontext.text: Why are bacterial cells treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium before transformation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Membrane Barrier
DNA is a hydrophilic, negatively charged macromolecule that cannot freely cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of bacterial membranes.

Step 2: Calcium Treatment
Divalent calcium ions (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}\)) shield negative charges on the DNA and membrane phospholipids, increasing the efficiency with which foreign DNA enters the bacterium through cell wall pores.

Final Answer:
Calcium treatment increases the permeability and efficiency with which DNA enters bacterial cells through wall pores.

answer.text: To neutralize the basic amino acids in bacterial ribosomal subunits
To increase the efficiency with which hydrophilic DNA enters through pores in the bacterial cell wall
To permanently disrupt the host bacterial chromosomal DNA
To activate DNA ligase enzymes present in the extracellular environment

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q27 - Temperature steps during transformation heat shock

questiontext.text: Which procedure correctly describes the heat shock method used to force recombinant DNA into competent bacterial cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Preparation
Competent bacterial cells and recombinant plasmid DNA are first incubated together on ice.

Step 2: Thermal Shock Cycle
The mixture is subjected to a brief heat shock at \(42^\circ\text{C}\) and immediately returned to ice, creating transient membrane pores that facilitate plasmid uptake.

Final Answer:
Heat shock involves incubating cells on ice, briefly exposing them to \(42^\circ\text{C}\), and returning them onto ice.

answer.text: Incubation at 100 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes followed by rapid freezing at -80 degrees Celsius
Continuous incubation in a water bath at 37 degrees Celsius for 24 hours
Incubation on ice, followed by a brief exposure to 42 degrees Celsius, and then placing them back on ice
Exposure to 72 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes followed by direct plating on ampicillin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q28 - Micro-injection method for gene transfer

questiontext.text: Which gene transfer method involves the direct mechanical injection of recombinant DNA into the nucleus of an animal cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Direct Delivery in Animal Cells
Various physical methods allow introduction of foreign genes into target host cells without using viral vectors.

Step 2: Micro-injection
Micro-injection utilizes a fine microscopic glass needle to directly introduce recombinant DNA directly into the nucleus of an individual animal cell.

Final Answer:
Micro-injection is the method of directly injecting recombinant DNA into the nucleus of an animal cell.

answer.text: Biolistics
Electroporation
Chemical transformation with calcium chloride
Micro-injection

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q29 - Microcarrier particles used in gene gun

questiontext.text: In the biolistics (gene gun) method commonly used for plant cell transformation, DNA is coated onto microscopic particles of which materials?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biolistics Principle
In biolistics, microscopic dense heavy-metal beads coated with exogenous DNA are accelerated at high velocity to penetrate plant cell walls.

Step 2: Particle Composition
The micro-particles used are specifically composed of inert, dense metals such as gold or tungsten.

Final Answer:
Micro-particles of gold or tungsten are coated with DNA in the biolistics method.

answer.text: Gold or tungsten
Iron or copper
Silver or platinum
Aluminium or zinc

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q30 - Enzymes used to eliminate cellular impurities

questiontext.text: During the isolation of pure DNA from cell lysates, which specific enzymes are sequentially employed to eliminate contaminating RNA and proteins?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Removal of Contaminants
Cell lysis releases nucleic acids along with proteins, RNA, lipids, and carbohydrates.

Step 2: Enzymatic Digestion
Contaminating RNA is degraded by treatment with ribonuclease, whereas contaminating proteins (including chromosomal histones) are digested by proteases, leaving purified DNA intact.

Final Answer:
Ribonuclease is used to eliminate RNA and protease is used to remove proteins.

answer.text: Cellulase and chitinase
Ribonuclease and protease
Lysozyme and DNA ligase
Endonuclease and exonuclease

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q31 - Thermostable DNA polymerase from Thermus aquaticus

questiontext.text: Why is the DNA polymerase isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus uniquely suited for the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Thermal Challenge in PCR
Repeated PCR cycles require heating the reaction mixture to approximately \(94^\circ\text{C}\) to denature double-stranded DNA into single strands.

Step 2: Taq Polymerase Adaptation
Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is thermostable and withstands this high denaturation temperature without denaturing or losing activity.

Final Answer:
Taq polymerase remains active through the high-temperature denaturation step of PCR.

answer.text: It functions optimally at 0 degrees Celsius to prevent DNA strand degradation
It does not require any oligonucleotide primers or dNTPs to synthesize DNA
It remains enzymatically active during the high-temperature denaturation step of double-stranded DNA
It cuts double-stranded DNA at palindromic recognition sites to yield sticky ends

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q32 - Nature and function of primers in PCR

questiontext.text: What are the primers utilized in a typical Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) mixture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role in DNA Synthesis
DNA polymerases require a free \(3'\)-OH group provided by a pre-existing strand to begin elongation.

Step 2: Primer Characteristics
In PCR, primers are pairs of short, chemically synthesized single-stranded oligonucleotides designed to anneal to complementary flanking sequences of the target DNA.

Final Answer:
PCR primers are small chemically synthesized oligonucleotides that are complementary to regions of the target DNA.

answer.text: Large circular plasmid molecules containing multiple restriction sites
Thermostable protein subunits that catalyze phosphodiester bond formation
Naturally occurring ribosomal RNA segments that bind to histones
Small chemically synthesized oligonucleotides complementary to the regions of template DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q33 - Three sequential steps of each PCR cycle

questiontext.text: What is the correct sequential order of the three main steps that occur during each cycle of Polymerase Chain Reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cycle Operation
PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence through repetitive thermal cycles.

Step 2: Order of Stages
Each cycle proceeds in three consecutive steps: first, thermal denaturation separates double-stranded DNA; second, primer annealing allows primers to bind to complementary sequences; and third, primer extension synthesizes the new complementary strands.

Final Answer:
The correct order of steps in each PCR cycle is denaturation, primer annealing, and extension of primers.

answer.text: Denaturation, primer annealing, and extension of primers
Primer annealing, denaturation, and ligation of ends
Extension of primers, denaturation, and spooling
Denaturation, insertional inactivation, and extension

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q34 - Advantage of sparged stirred-tank bioreactor

questiontext.text: In a sparged stirred-tank bioreactor, what is the specific advantage of sparging sterile air bubbles through the culture broth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Aeration Requirement
Large-scale aerobic cell culture demands continuous and efficient dissolution of oxygen into the liquid medium.

Step 2: Sparging Effect
Sparging sterile air into tiny bubbles exponentially increases the gas-liquid contact surface area, thereby maximizing oxygen transfer into the culture broth.

Final Answer:
Sparging sterile air bubbles dramatically increases the surface area for oxygen transfer.

answer.text: It decreases the temperature of the culture broth to halt bacterial replication
It dramatically increases the surface area for efficient oxygen transfer across the liquid
It selectively lyses contaminating anaerobic bacterial cells
It precipitates the synthesized recombinant protein at the bottom of the vessel

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q35 - Genetic engineering advantage over traditional breeding

questiontext.text: Why do recombinant DNA procedures overcome a major limitation inherent to traditional plant and animal hybridization breeding methods?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Limitation of Traditional Breeding
Classical hybridization shuffles entire parental genomes, frequently co-inheriting unwanted or deleterious traits along with target desirable alleles.

Step 2: Precision of Genetic Engineering
Recombinant DNA technology allows the isolation, cloning, and specific transfer of only one or a defined set of beneficial genes into the target organism without introducing undesirable traits.

Final Answer:
Genetic engineering allows isolation and introduction of only desired genes without introducing undesirable genes that accompany traditional breeding.

answer.text: Traditional breeding completely halts genetic variation, whereas recombinant DNA technology prevents sexual crossing entirely
Recombinant DNA techniques exclusively utilize eukaryotic organelles to synthesize bacterial antibodies
Traditional breeding leads to the multiplication of undesirable genes along with desired genes, whereas genetic engineering allows selective introduction of only desirable genes
Traditional breeding requires sterile bioreactor conditions, whereas recombinant DNA procedures are carried out without any enzymes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q36 - Fate of transferred alien DNA lacking ori

questiontext.text: If a piece of alien DNA without an origin of replication is transferred into a recipient bacterial cell without integrating into the host chromosome, what is its fate in subsequent generations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Replication Initiation
DNA replication cannot initiate spontaneously; it strictly requires a specific nucleotide sequence termed the origin of replication (ori) where the replisome machinery binds.

Step 2: Consequence of Missing Ori
An alien piece of DNA lacking an ori that does not integrate into the host chromosome cannot replicate in synchronization with cell division and is rapidly degraded or lost in daughter cells.

Final Answer:
The alien DNA cannot multiply autonomously and will be diluted out or lost in progeny cells.

answer.text: It will autonomously replicate at an exceptionally high copy number in all progeny cells
It will transform into a circular plasmid and induce tumor formation in the bacterium
It will immediately direct host ribosomes to synthesize foreign recombinant proteins
It will fail to multiply and will be progressively diluted or lost in the progeny cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q37 - Restriction endonuclease sites in vector pBR322

questiontext.text: In the standard Escherichia coli cloning vector pBR322, which pair of restriction endonuclease recognition sites is located within the ampicillin resistance gene (\(amp^R\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mapping pBR322
The genetic map of pBR322 features distinct restriction sites distributed across its selectable markers and structural sequences.

Step 2: Ampicillin Resistance Sites
The ampicillin resistance gene (\(amp^R\)) houses unique recognition sites for PstI and PvuI, whereas the tetracycline resistance gene (\(tet^R\)) contains sites for BamHI and SalI.

Final Answer:
PstI and PvuI are the restriction enzyme recognition sites located within the ampicillin resistance gene of pBR322.

answer.text: PstI and PvuI
BamHI and SalI
EcoRI and ClaI
HindIII and PvuII

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q38 - Replica plating selection of recombinant pBR322

questiontext.text: Foreign DNA was inserted into the BamHI site of pBR322 and transformed into recipient E. coli cells. After replica plating onto selective media, which growth profile distinguishes the recombinant transformants from non-recombinant transformants and non-transformants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Distinguishing Transformants
Non-transformants lack plasmid resistance and die on both antibiotics.

Step 2: Non-Recombinants vs Recombinants
Non-recombinants retain intact \(amp^R\) and \(tet^R\) genes, growing on both media. In recombinants, insertion at the BamHI site inactivates \(tet^R\); hence, they survive on ampicillin plates but cannot grow when transferred to tetracycline plates.

Final Answer:
Recombinant transformants grow on ampicillin-containing medium but fail to grow on medium containing tetracycline.

answer.text: Grow on tetracycline medium, but fail to grow on ampicillin medium
Grow on ampicillin medium, but fail to grow on tetracycline medium
Grow simultaneously on both ampicillin and tetracycline media
Fail to grow on both ampicillin and tetracycline media

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q39 - Screening recombinants using chromogenic substrate mechanism

questiontext.text: Why is screening recombinants using insertional inactivation of \(\beta\)-galactosidase considered superior to antibiotic-based selection in pBR322?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Limitation of Dual Antibiotic Selection
Selecting recombinants via antibiotic resistance disruption requires plating on one antibiotic followed by replica plating onto a second antibiotic plate, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming.

Step 2: Advantage of Chromogenic Selection
Insertional inactivation of \(\beta\)-galactosidase resolves recombinant (white) from non-recombinant (blue) colonies directly on a single plate containing a chromogenic substrate.

Final Answer:
Chromogenic screening differentiates recombinants directly on a single plate, avoiding the cumbersome dual-plating required by antibiotic inactivation.

answer.text: Because \(\beta\)-galactosidase actively eliminates non-transformants by digesting their peptidoglycan walls
Because antibiotic selection requires expensive thermostable polymerases and radioactive probes
Because antibiotic inactivation requires cumbersome replica plating on two different antibiotic plates, whereas chromogenic screening distinguishes colonies on a single plate
Because chromogenic selection produces bright orange fluorescence under ultraviolet irradiation without any substrate

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q40 - Consequence of multiple recognition sites in vector

questiontext.text: Why is it essential that a cloning vector possesses only one, or very few, recognition sites for a given restriction endonuclease?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Digestion Dynamics
A single recognition site allows the circular vector to be linearized cleanly without fragmentation, leaving cohesive ends ready for foreign DNA insertion.

Step 2: Impact of Multiple Sites
If multiple target sites exist within the vector, digestion cuts the vector into multiple small fragments, which drastically complicates ligation and prevents the formation of intact recombinant plasmids.

Final Answer:
Multiple recognition sites cut the vector into numerous fragments, severely complicating gene cloning.

answer.text: Because multiple recognition sites prevent DNA ligase from forming hydrogen bonds
Because multiple recognition sites permanently inactivate the origin of replication
Because multiple recognition sites induce hyper-methylation of host genomic DNA
Because multiple recognition sites will cleave the vector into several fragments, complicating the gene cloning process

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q41 - Theoretical amplification after thirty PCR cycles

questiontext.text: If a single double-stranded DNA template molecule undergoes 30 complete cycles of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), approximately how many target DNA copies are synthesized?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Exponential Amplification Principle
In PCR, each cycle doubles the quantity of target DNA, following the geometric progression \(N = N_0 \times 2^n\), where \(n\) is the number of cycles.

Step 2: Calculation for Thirty Cycles
For \(N_0 = 1\) and \(n = 30\), \(2^{30} = 1,073,741,824\), which corresponds to approximately 1 billion copies (\(10^9\)).

Final Answer:
Thirty cycles of PCR yield approximately one billion (\(10^9\)) copies of the target DNA fragment.

answer.text: Approximately \(1 \times 10^9\) (one billion) copies
Approximately \(1 \times 10^6\) (one million) copies
Approximately \(30 \times 10^3\) (thirty thousand) copies
Approximately 60 copies

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q42 - Importance of primer annealing temperature conditions

questiontext.text: During PCR, what would occur if the temperature during the primer annealing step is set too high, exceeding the melting temperature of the primers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Annealing Step Mechanism
Annealing involves lowering the temperature so that oligonucleotide primers can form hydrogen bonds with their complementary regions on single-stranded template DNA.

Step 2: Consequence of Excessive Temperature
If the temperature remains above the melting temperature (\(T_m\)) of the primers, thermal kinetic energy prevents stable base pairing, preventing primer annealing and thus halting extension.

Final Answer:
Excessively high annealing temperatures prevent primers from binding to the complementary regions on the template DNA.

answer.text: Taq polymerase would permanently lose its enzymatic activity due to irreversible denaturation
Primers would fail to anneal specifically to their complementary target sequences, preventing extension
Double-stranded DNA molecules would fail to separate into single-stranded templates
Deoxyribonucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) would undergo spontaneous hydrolysis into cyclic AMP

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q43 - Expression of recombinant protein in heterologous host

questiontext.text: In recombinant DNA technology, what defines a 'recombinant protein'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heterologous Expression
Recombinant DNA molecules carrying target genes are transferred into recipient host systems such as bacteria, yeast, or animal cell cultures.

Step 2: Definition
When a protein-encoding foreign gene is transcribed and translated inside a host of a different species (a heterologous host), the produced functional polypeptide is termed a recombinant protein.

Final Answer:
A recombinant protein is a protein encoded by a gene that is expressed in a heterologous host.

answer.text: Any protein synthesized by chemical peptide synthesis in an abiotic cell-free system
A structural histone protein extracted directly from human chromatin suspensions
A protein encoded by a foreign gene expressed inside a heterologous host organism
An endogenous bacterial enzyme modified by the addition of methyl functional groups

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q44 - Continuous culture maintenance of active log phase

questiontext.text: How does a continuous culture system in industrial bioprocessing achieve higher biomass and maximum product yields compared to a closed batch culture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Batch vs Continuous Culture
In closed batch culture, nutrients deplete and toxic wastes build up, causing cells to transition from exponential growth into stationary and death phases.

Step 2: Continuous Culture Advantage
A continuous culture continuously feeds fresh nutrient medium while removing spent medium, maintaining the cell population in its physiologically most active exponential (log) phase to maximize biomass and recombinant protein yield.

Final Answer:
A continuous culture maintains cells in their active log/exponential phase by continuously replenishing fresh medium and draining used medium.

answer.text: By maintaining cells continuously in the stationary phase where secondary metabolites accumulate
By allowing toxic metabolic by-products to accumulate to trigger cellular apoptosis
By repeatedly exposing the cell culture to high temperatures to stimulate heat shock proteins
By draining used medium from one side while simultaneously adding fresh medium from the other to maintain cells in their exponential log phase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q45 - Operational advantages of stirred tank bioreactor

questiontext.text: What fundamental design feature enables a stirred-tank bioreactor to support large culture volumes (100–1000 litres) that shake flasks cannot provide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Limitation of Flasks
Simple laboratory shake flasks cannot maintain optimal conditions or provide adequate aeration in volumes exceeding a few litres.

Step 2: Bioreactor Engineering
A stirred-tank bioreactor features a motor-driven impeller for uniform mixing and aeration, combined with automated controls for temperature, pH, foam, steam sterilization, and sterile sampling ports to scale up production to 100-1000 litres.

Final Answer:
Stirred-tank bioreactors feature integrated agitation, aeration, pH and temperature controls, and sampling ports required for large volumes.

answer.text: Integrated systems for uniform mixing, oxygen delivery, temperature, pH, foam control, and periodic sampling ports
The absence of any internal moving parts or agitation systems to avoid shear stress
Direct reliance on manual swirling of the cylindrical vessel at periodic intervals
Exclusive use of anaerobic fermentative pathways that do not require any dissolved oxygen

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q46 - Downstream processing components and quality control

questiontext.text: Which processes are collectively categorized under downstream processing in recombinant DNA technology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Biosynthetic vs Downstream Phase
The biosynthetic stage involves culturing host cells in bioreactors to produce the target molecule.

Step 2: Downstream Components
Once synthesis is complete, downstream processing encompasses product recovery through separation, purification, addition of suitable preservatives, and rigorous quality control testing or clinical trials before commercial marketing.

Final Answer:
Downstream processing comprises the separation and purification of the biosynthetic product, along with formulation with preservatives and quality control.

answer.text: Ligation of gene of interest with vector DNA and transformation of competent hosts
Separation, purification of the product, formulation with preservatives, and clinical testing
In vitro amplification of target DNA through automated thermal cycles in PCR
Enzymatic restriction digestion of genomic DNA followed by agarose gel electrophoresis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q47 - Requirement of cutting vector and source DNA identically

questiontext.text: Why must both the foreign donor DNA and the cloning vector be cleaved by the identical restriction endonuclease during recombinant DNA construction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Specificity of Cleavage
Each restriction endonuclease cleaves DNA at a unique palindromic sequence, generating a characteristic single-stranded overhang.

Step 2: Compatibility Requirement
Cleaving both source DNA and plasmid vector with the identical enzyme produces matching, mutually complementary sticky ends, allowing hydrogen bonding and efficient covalent sealing by DNA ligase.

Final Answer:
Cutting both DNA molecules with the same restriction enzyme produces identical complementary sticky ends necessary for ligation.

answer.text: To prevent the host bacterial cell from recognizing the vector as an infectious viral agent
To ensure that both molecules acquire identical molecular weights and sedimentation coefficients
To generate matching complementary sticky ends that can form hydrogen bonds before DNA ligase action
To prevent DNA polymerase from duplicating the alien DNA prior to host transformation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q48 - Mechanism of disarmed pathogen gene delivery

questiontext.text: How do disarmed pathogen vectors transfer recombinant DNA into eukaryotic host cells without causing disease?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Natural Pathogen Ingress
Pathogens such as Agrobacterium tumefaciens and retroviruses have evolved specialized mechanisms to infect host cells and integrate genetic material into host genomes.

Step 2: Disarming Strategy
By genetically deleting the pathogenic/oncogenic genes while retaining the natural infection apparatus, researchers harness these natural delivery vehicles to ferry desirable therapeutic or agronomic genes into host cells safely.

Final Answer:
Disarmed pathogens use their natural infection mechanisms to transfer recombinant DNA into host cells after their disease-causing genes have been disabled or replaced.

answer.text: They inject toxic metabolites that paralyze host defense mechanisms while leaving viral DNA outside
They fuse with mitochondrial membranes to direct transcription of cellular respiration enzymes
They utilize mechanical particle bombardment to physically tear open nuclear membranes
They utilize their natural infection and cell-entry mechanisms while the deleted virulence genes are replaced by genes of interest
